patterns.title: -eur, -ier, -ien, -iste, -ant: the person
patterns.explanation: Add one of these endings to a verb or a thing, and you get the person who does that job or activity. Listen for the ending at the end of a job word.
patterns.tip: Feminine forms: vendeuse, cuisinière, pharmacienne, étudiante. Words ending in -iste stay the same: la dentiste.

patterns.title: in-, im-, mé-: the opposite
patterns.explanation: Put in-, im- or mé- at the front of a describing word and it means 'not'. Use im- before p or b.
patterns.tip: The word's meaning flips, but its gender and endings stay the same: impatient, impatiente.

patterns.title: -er makes the verb
patterns.explanation: Add -er (or -iser) to a noun or a describing word to make a verb: doing the thing. Most French verbs end in -er.
patterns.tip: -er verbs are the most regular kind, so they are the easiest to conjugate.

patterns.title: re-: again or back
patterns.explanation: re- at the start of a verb means doing it again or going back. Take off the re- and you often find a verb you already know.

patterns.title: Verb minus -er, or plus -ée: the noun
patterns.explanation: Cut the verb ending, or change -er to -ée, and you get the noun for the action or the moment: arriver gives l'arrivée.
patterns.tip: Nouns ending in -ée are almost always feminine: l'arrivée, l'entrée (but le musée).

patterns.title: -age: the thing or the action
patterns.explanation: -age turns a verb or a noun into a noun for the action, the result, or a whole set of something: passer gives le passage.
patterns.tip: Nouns ending in -age are almost always masculine: le mariage, le paysage.

patterns.title: Two words hidden in one
patterns.explanation: Some everyday words are two short words glued together. Split them and the meaning often shows: bon + jour = good day.

patterns.title: Two words joined with a hyphen
patterns.explanation: A hyphen (-) joins two words into one new noun. The first word often describes the second: grand + mère = grandmother.
patterns.tip: grand- and petit- make family words: grand-père, petit-fils.

patterns.title: X de Y, X à Y: a thing of or for
patterns.explanation: de (of) or à (for) links two nouns into one name. The main thing comes first and the detail comes after: sac à main = bag for the hand.
patterns.tip: The gender comes from the first word: la pomme de terre, le sac à main.

patterns.title: Action + object: the tool
patterns.explanation: A verb (lave, sèche, tourne, porte) plus the thing it works on names the tool or machine that does the job: lave-linge washes laundry.
patterns.tip: These tool words are usually masculine: le lave-linge, le tournevis.

patterns.title: a-, ap-, em-, com-, sou-: new verbs
patterns.explanation: A short prefix on a verb you know makes a related verb. porter (carry) gives apporter (bring here) and emporter (take away).

patterns.title: Past form as a word: -é, -t, -is
patterns.explanation: The past form of a verb (fermé, ouvert, pris) can be used on its own as a describing word or a noun: fermer gives fermé (closed).
patterns.tip: -er verbs make it with -é. Add -e for feminine: fermée, ouverte, prise.
